526.title: Sita's argument
526.hook: Rama asks Sita to stay behind, and she makes her case
526.howItsDone: Sita is honored in Hindu devotion as Rama's companion, and in this scene the text gives the choice to share his exile to her, in her own voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm, toward blame. Don't blame Kaikeyi, he said; this is daiva, and no blame for anyone. Did you fix something before looking for whose fault it was? A new week begins, and Sita speaks. Day five hundred twenty-six.

Rama comes home with his news, and with a plan for Sita. She's going to stay in Ayodhya and wait for him. He has thought it through, kindly, carefully, and alone. In Valmiki's telling, Sita is many things in this scene, and quiet isn't the first of them. Valmiki gives her the floor, and she uses it. She hears the whole plan out. Then, piece by piece, she takes it apart.
screen: `RAMA'S PLAN FOR SITA.` → `KINDLY, CAREFULLY, ALONE.` → `SHE TAKES THE PLAN APART.`

segments.voice: Sita has been waiting at home for the procession. She sees Rama come in alone, pale, with no royal umbrella and no music, and she knows something is wrong. He tells her everything. Then he gives her instructions. Stay here. Serve my father and my mothers. Don't praise me in front of Bharata, because men in power don't like hearing others praised. Keep your vows, live simply, and wait for me. Valmiki says Sita answers out of love and anger together. Her first point is sharp. Father, mother, brother, son, each lives out their own fortune, she says. But a wife shares her husband's. If you've been sent to the forest, so have I. Her second point is practical. If you go into the forest today, I'll walk ahead of you, trampling the thorns and the sharp grass so your path is easier. Her third point is about what she wants. She'd rather be in the forest with him than in a palace without him. She's not asking for permission to suffer. She's describing the forest as a place she wants to see: the mountains, the lakes, the lotus ponds, the birds. She'll be happy there, she says, as long as he's there. Notice the shape of it. Rama made a decision for both of them, kindly and alone. Sita refuses to be decided for. Valmiki gives her the room to make it, at length, in her own voice, and she isn't finished yet.
screen: `NO UMBRELLA, NO MUSIC.` · `RAMA'S PLAN: STAY HERE.` · `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S FORTUNE.` · `I'LL WALK AHEAD, TRAMPLING THORNS.` · then, large: `SITA REFUSES TO BE DECIDED FOR.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Think of a decision someone made for you, out of kindness, without asking. Notice how that felt. Now think of one you've made for someone else the same way. Let both sit side by side. On each breath out, imagine handing the question back to the other person, open, so they can answer it in their own voice. The bell holds the time.
Sita's argument. Asked to stay behind, she answers out of love and anger: a wife shares her husband's fortune, and she'll walk ahead of him through the thorns.
Your line: I'll walk ahead, trampling thorns. Today, before you decide something for someone you love, ask them what they want. Day five hundred twenty-six.

527.title: Sita's argument
527.hook: Rama lists every danger in the forest, and Sita answers with one sharp question
527.howItsDone: Valmiki keeps Sita's rebuke sharp, and the scene shows her going to the forest by her own choice, against her husband's first wish.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's argument, part one. A wife shares her husband's fortune, she said, and she'd walk ahead through the thorns. Did you ask someone what they wanted before deciding for them? Today Rama tries again, and so does she. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

How do you stop someone you love from following you into danger, without forbidding it? Rama tries a list. Every hardship the forest holds, named one by one. It's love, mostly. It's also a way of winning without saying no. He has watched his father break and his mother weep today, and he wants one person he loves kept safe. He means every word. And Sita, who has been patient, finally runs out of patience.
screen: `THE LIST OF DANGERS.` → `WINNING WITHOUT SAYING NO.` → `SITA LOSES HER PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: The forest is hard, Rama says. Lions roar from mountain caves. Rivers are full of crocodiles and hard to cross. You sleep on fallen leaves on the ground. You eat whatever fruit you find, or nothing. Wind, darkness, hunger, snakes, scorpions, thorns. Stay here. Sita answers his list one item at a time. With you, she says, the hardships become comforts. The grass will feel like a soft blanket. The fruit you bring me will taste like nectar. And she adds something new. When I was a girl in my father's house, she says, people who read the signs told my family that one day I would live in a forest. I've wanted to see it ever since. Then Rama still hesitates, and she says something with a sting in it. What was my father thinking, she asks, when he chose as his son-in-law a woman in the form of a man? It's a hard thing to say, and Valmiki doesn't soften it. Sita is accusing Rama of failing at the one thing a protector is for: keeping her with him. Then she breaks down and weeps. And Rama gives way. He holds her and says: I didn't know your mind. I wouldn't want heaven itself without you. Come with me. Give away your things, and let's go. It's worth noticing who wins this argument. In a story about a son obeying his father's word without a question, the wife questions, pushes, and changes her husband's mind. Valmiki honors both.

segments.voice: Sit and settle into the breath. Think of a time someone changed your mind, maybe sharply, and they were right. Let the memory come back, even the sting of it. Breathe in, and feel the moment you resisted. Breathe out, and feel the moment you gave way. Stay with the gratitude, if it's there, for someone who loved you enough to argue. The bell holds the time.

528.title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
528.hook: the loyal younger brother says out loud what everyone else is only thinking
528.howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for a brother's devotion; this outburst in Kausalya's room shows that devotion as anger, before it learns restraint.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's argument, won. She answered every danger, rebuked Rama, and he said: come with me. Did you let someone change your mind? Today we step back into Kausalya's room, where someone has been burning. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

We've watched Rama be calm for days now. It would be easy to think everyone in the palace felt the way he did. Valmiki makes sure we don't. When Rama told his mother the news, Lakshmana was standing in the room. He'd been silent. Then, while Kausalya wept, he spoke, and what came out was the question the story has been holding back. This is wrong. Somebody should stop it. Why isn't anybody stopping it?
screen: `NOT EVERYONE IS CALM.` → `LAKSHMANA, SILENT IN THE ROOM.` → `WHY ISN'T ANYBODY STOPPING IT?`

segments.voice: Lakshmana's anger has several layers, and Valmiki lets us hear all of them. First, it's about fairness. Rama has done nothing wrong. Who in the whole kingdom can name a single fault in him? To throw him out for no reason is against dharma itself. Second, it's about the king. Lakshmana says what no one else will say: the old man has been ruled by his desire for a young wife, and he isn't fit to judge. He goes further still, with words against his own father that Valmiki records and we won't repeat here. Third, it's about action. I'm armed, Lakshmana tells Rama. I'm with you. If anyone in this city takes Bharata's side, I'll fight them all. Let Kausalya see it. Let the whole world see it. It's frightening, and it's also loyal. Every word of it comes from love for his brother. Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for his devotion to his brother. That devotion, today, looks like a drawn bow. Kausalya, desperate, actually seizes on it. Listen to your brother, she tells Rama. Don't go. And this is a harder test of Rama's calm than Kaikeyi was. Not by Kaikeyi, who is his opponent, but by Lakshmana, who is on his side, offering him exactly what part of him might want. The rage is real, it's righteous, and it's within reach. Tomorrow, we hear Lakshmana's argument at its strongest, and what Rama does with it.
screen: `RAMA HAS DONE NOTHING WRONG.` · `THE OLD KING ISN'T FIT TO JUDGE.` · `I'M ARMED. I'M WITH YOU.` · `RAMA'S CALM, TESTED BY A FRIEND.` · then, large: `THE RAGE IS REAL, AND IT'S LOYAL.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath slow. Remember a time you were angry on someone else's behalf, at an injustice done to a friend or a family member. Let a little of that heat come back. Notice where it lives in the body: chest, hands, face. Don't push it away. On each breath out, notice the love underneath it, the care that made you angry in the first place. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana, Rama's loyal younger brother. Loyal to the bone, he says Rama has done no wrong and offers to fight the whole city for him.
Your line: I'm armed, I'm with you. Today, if you get angry for someone, find the love underneath it before you act. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

529.title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
529.hook: only the weak blame fate, Lakshmana says, and then he has to decide what to do with his strength
529.carry: the rage stays, he doesn't spend it
529.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often set Rama's speech on daiva, fate, beside Lakshmana's speech on purushakara, human effort, and leave listeners to weigh both.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's rage and restraint, part one, the rage. Rama has done nothing wrong, he said, and I'll fight for him. Did you find the love underneath an anger? Today, the argument and the restraint. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

A few days ago, Rama told Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi, because what had happened was daiva, something larger than any one person. It's a gentle idea. Lakshmana hates it. He's standing with his brow knotted, and Valmiki says he's breathing hard, like an angry snake in its hole. And he answers his brother with an argument that people have been quoting ever since. It's the other side of the old question: how much is fate, and how much is up to us?
screen: `DAIVA, RAMA SAID.` → `LAKSHMANA HATES IT.` → `HOW MUCH IS UP TO US?`

segments.voice: Here is Lakshmana's case. Fate, he says, is what weak people talk about. The brave and strong don't sit waiting for it. A real hero pushes fate aside with his own effort. If you call this fate, you're giving up before you've even tried. Then he holds up his arms. These aren't for decoration, he says. They're for protecting you. Today the people will see which is stronger, fate or me. Let me take the kingdom for you, and you rule it. It's a powerful speech, and Valmiki doesn't make it foolish. In Hindu thought, effort, purushakara, is honored just as seriously as fate. Plenty of teachers would side with Lakshmana's view on another day. But listen to what Rama does. He doesn't argue the philosophy again. He wipes away Lakshmana's tears, and speaks to him as a brother. Know that I am determined to keep our father's word, he says. Stand with me in this. That's the whole answer. And Lakshmana listens. The text describes him with his head lowered, still grieving, still angry, and silent. This is the restraint in his name today. He doesn't stop feeling the rage. He chooses not to spend it. He has the arms, the bow, the courage, and probably the soldiers. What he gives his brother is the thing that's hardest for a strong person to give: holding back. And immediately, the energy has somewhere to go. If you're going to the forest, Lakshmana says, then so am I.
screen: `ONLY THE WEAK TALK OF FATE.` · `THESE ARMS ARE FOR YOU.` · `RAMA WIPES AWAY HIS TEARS.` · `THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.` · then, large: `THEN SO AM I.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the body be heavy. Close your hands into loose fists, and feel your own strength in them. Hold them like that for a few breaths. Then, slowly, open them, palms up, resting on your knees. Notice that the strength is still there in the open hands. Breathe with them open. Holding back isn't the same as being weak. The bell holds the time.
Purushakara, human effort, the old partner and rival of fate. Lakshmana argues that heroes push fate aside, then lowers his head, keeps his strength unspent, and chooses to go with Rama.
Your line: the rage stays, he doesn't spend it. Today, when you could win by force, try opening your hands instead. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

530.title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
530.hook: Lakshmana asks to go, and the text is silent about the wife he leaves behind
530.carry: a bow, a spade and a basket
530.howItsDone: Later poets and storytellers have written about Urmila, Lakshmana's wife, whom Valmiki barely mentions; some retellings give her a sacrifice of her own during the fourteen years.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's rage and restraint, part two. He argued that heroes push fate aside, then lowered his head and held back. Did you try opening your hands? Today, his rage becomes a job. Day five hundred thirty.
screen: `THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana was in the room while Sita won her argument. He heard her say she'd walk ahead of Rama through the thorns. Now he has his own case to make, and it sounds like a sibling who turns up on moving day without being asked and heads straight for the heaviest boxes. It isn't eloquent. It's practical: who carries what, who walks where, who finds the food. And it ends with a job.
screen: `HE HEARD SITA WIN.` → `CARRYING THE HEAVY BOXES.` → `PRACTICAL, NOT ELOQUENT.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana falls at Rama's feet, with tears in his eyes, and asks to go. Rama says no, at first, and gives a good reason. Someone has to look after our mothers, Kausalya and Sumitra. The king is consumed by Kaikeyi now, and Bharata may not care for them. Lakshmana has an answer. Bharata will honor them, he says, and if he doesn't, I'll deal with him. Kausalya has lands and wealth enough to support a thousand like me. Then comes the practical part. I'll walk ahead of you with my bow. I'll carry a spade and a basket. I'll find the path, gather the fruit and roots, and do the work, while you and Sita enjoy the mountains. Rama is moved, and says yes. Then he gives Lakshmana a job. At Janaka's great sacrifice, the god Varuna gave us divine bows, armor, quivers and swords. They're being kept at our teacher's house. Go and bring them. Lakshmana goes. So the rage that wanted to fight the city becomes a younger brother carrying weapons for protection, a spade for digging, and a basket for fruit. That's the restraint finished: not anger erased, but anger given work. And here is something the text doesn't say. Lakshmana is married. On the same day Rama married Sita, he married Sita's sister Urmila. Valmiki doesn't tell us what Lakshmana said to her, or what she said to him, or whether she asked to come. He's silent. Later poets and storytellers noticed that silence, and some have filled it in their own ways. Valmiki leaves the space empty.
screen: `LAKSHMANA FALLS AT RAMA'S FEET.` · `WHO WILL CARE FOR OUR MOTHERS?` · `A BOW, A SPADE AND A BASKET.` · `ANGER GIVEN WORK.` · then, large: `AND URMILA? THE TEXT IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone whose sacrifice in your life went mostly unspoken: someone who stayed behind, covered for you, kept things running while you were away. Bring their face to mind. On each breath in, remember something specific they did. On each breath out, send them thanks, even silently, even if they'll never hear it. The bell holds the time.
Urmila, Lakshmana's wife, Sita's sister, married the same day, left in a silence Valmiki never fills. The anger that wanted to fight becomes a brother walking ahead with a bow, a spade and a basket.
Your line: a bow, a spade and a basket. Today, give one frustration a practical job to do. Day five hundred thirty.

531.title: the departure
531.hook: before he leaves, Rama gives everything away, and makes a poor old man throw his stick
531.howItsDone: Hindus give dana, gifts, at turning points such as rites, festivals and journeys; in the text, Rama gives before he leaves, and the Trijata episode is a light moment in a dark book.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana's rage and restraint, complete. A bow, a spade and a basket, and Urmila left in silence. Did you give one frustration a job? Today the departure begins, with giving. Day five hundred thirty-one.
screen: `A BOW, A SPADE AND A BASKET.`

segments.voice: Armlets. Earrings. A golden girdle. A herd of cows. On the day Rama leaves, his rooms empty out, piece by piece, into other people's hands. Leaving a home can come with a day like this: the couch to a cousin, the plants to whoever will water them, sad and oddly freeing at once. Here it's a prince's wealth. And in the middle of it, Valmiki tells a small story with a joke in it, on a day built for tears.
screen: `ARMLETS, EARRINGS, COWS.` → `A PRINCE'S WEALTH, GIVEN AWAY.` → `A JOKE ON A DAY OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Rama sends for Suyajna, the son of his teacher Vasishtha, and gives him armlets, earrings and jewels. Sita sends a necklace and a golden girdle to Suyajna's wife. Gifts go to teachers, to the brahmins who taught the princes, to the old servants of the household, to people who depend on Rama for their living, so that nobody is left without support while he's gone. Then the story. Near Ayodhya lives a very poor brahmin named Trijata. He's old and thin and spends his days digging in the fields with a spade, scraping a living. His wife, hearing that Rama is giving things away, says to him: go. Maybe he'll give you something. So Trijata comes and stands before the prince. And Rama, of all things, teases him. I haven't yet given away even a thousand of my cows, he says. Throw your staff. However far it lands, every cow up to that point is yours. The old man ties up his clothes, swings his staff with every bit of strength he has, and throws. It flies across the river Sarayu and lands in a pasture full of cattle. Rama embraces him and gives him every cow up to that spot. And then he apologizes. Don't be offended, he says. It was a joke. I only wanted to see the strength in you. It's a tiny scene. But look at what it shows. On the day his life is falling apart, Rama is still generous, still playful, still paying attention to one poor man's dignity. Grief hasn't made him small.
screen: `GIFTS SO NO ONE IS LEFT WITHOUT.` · `TRIJATA, OLD, POOR, WITH A SPADE.` · `THROW YOUR STAFF.` · `IT WAS A JOKE. FORGIVE ME.` · then, large: `GRIEF HASN'T MADE HIM SMALL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Look around in your mind at what you own: the room you're in, the things on the shelves. Pick one thing you could give away this week, to someone who'd use it. Picture handing it over. Notice how it feels to let it go. Then rest in the breath, lighter by one thing. The bell holds the time.
The departure, part one: giving. Rama and Sita give away their wealth, and Rama makes poor Trijata throw his staff, and gives him every cow up to where it lands.
Your line: throw your staff. Today, give one thing away, and if you can, make the person laugh while you do it. Day five hundred thirty-one.

532.title: the departure
532.hook: bark clothes are brought out, Sita doesn't know how to put them on, and Lakshmana's mother gives him one verse
532.carry: think of the forest as Ayodhya
532.howItsDone: Sumitra's verse, rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi, is recited and taught as a picture of how love can make any place home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure, part one. Gifts for everyone, and an old man's staff flying across the river. Did you give something away? Today, the goodbyes, and the end of a week. Day five hundred thirty-two.

Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk to the palace on foot. Crowds line the streets, and Valmiki lets us hear them. People who were cheering for the coronation this morning are weeping now, and some are openly criticizing the king. Inside, the whole family is waiting: the old king, the queens, counselors, priests. This is the last room before the road. And someone has brought a pile of clothes made of tree bark.
screen: `THEY WALK TO THE PALACE.` → `THE CROWDS WEEP.` → `A PILE OF BARK CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha begs Rama, one last time, to stay just one night. Rama gently refuses. The king orders the army and the treasury to go with him. Kaikeyi objects, and Rama himself turns it down: why keep the rope, he asks, once you've given away the elephant? Then Kaikeyi hands out the bark garments. Rama and Lakshmana take off their fine clothes and put them on. Sita takes one, and stands holding it, confused. She has never worn anything like it. Valmiki tells us she doesn't know how to tie it, and tries, and can't, and is ashamed, and starts to cry. Rama ties it for her, over her silk. Valmiki lets the moment stay small and plain. Vasishtha, watching, finally loses his temper with Kaikeyi. Sita was never part of the boons, he says. She doesn't need to wear bark. And the king orders that Sita be given clothes and jewels enough for all fourteen years. Then the mothers speak. Kausalya counsels Sita. And Sumitra, Lakshmana's mother, gives her son one verse: rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi māṃ viddhi janakātmajām, ayodhyām aṭavīṃ viddhi, gaccha tāta yathāsukham. Think of Rama as your father Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya. Go, my son, and go happily. Look back at this week. Sita argued and won. Lakshmana raged, then held back, then took up a spade. Gifts were given. And now a mother sends her son into exile by telling him he isn't leaving home at all.
screen: `STAY ONE NIGHT. NO.` · `SITA CAN'T TIE THE BARK.` · `VASISHTHA: SITA WASN'T IN THE BOONS.` · `SUMITRA: THE FOREST IS AYODHYA.` · then, large: `RĀMAṂ DAŚARATHAṂ VIDDHI.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Sumitra told her son: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Try it with wherever you are. On a breath in, notice this room, this chair, this light. On a breath out, let it be home for these two minutes, nothing to escape from, nothing missing. If your mind goes to somewhere else you'd rather be, gently bring it back here, and call this home again. The bell holds the time.
The departure, part two: the goodbyes. Bark clothes, Rama tying Sita's, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya.
Your line: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Today, wherever you end up, try calling it home for a minute. Day five hundred thirty-two.

fork.setup: you're Sumitra. your son is leaving for fourteen years in the forest with his brother. what do you tell him?
options: come back as soon as you can.
think of Rama as your father, Sita as me, the forest as Ayodhya.
watch out for Kaikeyi's people.
fork.reveal: her verse tells him he isn't leaving home: home goes with him.

original.note: Sanskrit valkala: bark, and clothing made of bark, worn by forest ascetics.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sumitra just says goodbye.
what it means: she tells Lakshmana that Rama is his father, Sita his mother and the forest his home.
what a scholar hears: some commentators also read the verse a second way, with Rama as Vishnu and Sita as Lakshmi, so that the forest becomes heaven itself.
